citations.quote: For an integer $n\ge2$, put $T_n=\mathbb R^2/(n\mathbb Z)^2$, with horizontal circles $\alpha_i=\{y=i\}$ and vertical circles $\beta_j=\{x=j\}$ for $i,j\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$. A **toroidal grid diagram of grid number $n$** is a pair of disjoint sets $\mathbb O,\mathbb X$ of points in the open cells of this grid such that every row and every column contains exactly one point of each set. At each crossing of the projected link, the vertical segment is over and the horizontal segment is under. Orient each horizontal segment from its $O$-marking to its $X$-marking and each vertical segment from its $X$-marking to its $O$-marking. The markings and these segments determine an oriented link. Following each component from an $O$ along its row to an $X$ and then along that column to the next $O$ defines a permutation of the $n$ $O$-markings; its cycles are the link components. The grid represents a knot precisely when this permutation is one $n$-cycle.

derivations.claim: Stabilize the marking $\bar b$ at $(Q,H)$ by replacing it with $\bar b$ at $(U,H)$, $\bar b$ at $(Q,J)$, and $b$ at $(U,J)$. The cell $(Q,H)$ is empty. In the block with north row $H$, south row $J$, west column $Q$, and east column $U$, its northwest cell is empty, northeast and southwest have $\bar b$, and southeast has $b$. Row $H$ still pairs $b$ with $\bar b$, row $J$ pairs $\bar b$ with $b$, column $Q$ still pairs $\bar b$ with its unchanged exterior $b$, and column $U$ pairs $\bar b$ with $b$. All other rows and columns retain their two types. This is exactly a stabilization of type $\bar b:\mathrm{NW}$ and gives stage 1.

At stage 1, the closed vertical interval of $U$ is $[J,H]$. The interval of $R$ starts at its lower partner row and ends at $K$. Its endpoints satisfy $\text{lower partner}<J<H<K$, so $[J,H]$ lies strictly inside it. The two columns are adjacent by their order in the table. Their exchange is an allowed nested-interval commutation and gives stage 2. This reasoning does not depend on either marking type.

At stage 2, row $H$ has endpoints $P,U$ and row $K$ has endpoints $L,R$. The column order is $P<L<Q<R<U$, so $[L,R]$ lies strictly inside $[P,U]$. The rows are adjacent. Their exchange is therefore an allowed nested-interval commutation, giving stage 3.

At stage 3 the vertical interval of $P$ is $[H,T]$. Those of $L,R$ end at $K<H$, and that of $Q$ ends at $J<H$; all begin at their lower partner rows. Hence each is disjoint as a closed interval from $[H,T]$. Commute $P$ with its adjacent neighbor $L$, then with $Q$, then with $R$. At each exchange these same labeled intervals remain disjoint, and the adjacent-column orders are successively $L,P,Q,R,U$, $L,Q,P,R,U$, and $L,Q,R,P,U$. This proves the fourth table arrow as three allowed commutations, not a single nonadjacent-column move.

At stage 4 the closed horizontal intervals of rows $K,H$ are respectively $[L,R]$ and $[P,U]$. The column order $L<Q<R<P<U$ makes them disjoint, including their endpoints. They are adjacent rows. Their exchange is an allowed disjoint-interval commutation and gives stage 5, with $J<H<K$.

At stage 5 the adjacent rows $J,H$ and adjacent columns $P,U$ contain $b$ in $(P,H)$ and $(U,J)$, $\bar b$ in $(U,H)$, and an empty $(P,J)$. The other marking in row $J$ is $\bar b$ in column $Q$ outside this block, and the other marking in column $P$ is $\bar b$ in row $T$ outside it. Thus this is a $b:\mathrm{SW}$ stabilization block in reverse. Contract it, deleting row $H$ and column $U$, and put $b$ in $(P,J)$. The remaining marking $(Q,J)$ has type $\bar b$. Every retained row and column again has one marking of each type. This proves stage 6 and the claimed finite move word. The only altered exterior coordinates are exactly those moved by the stated full row and column exchanges; nothing about arbitrary exterior markings was assumed.

Initially the horizontal $H$ segment between $P$ and $Q$ crosses column $L$, whose upper endpoint is at $K>H$, but not column $R$. Finally the $J$ segment between $Q$ and $P$ crosses column $R$, whose upper endpoint is at $K>J$, but not $L$. The overpassing cap consists of the vertical legs $L,R$ and their horizontal segment at $K$; the relative order of the three lower legs $L,Q,R$ is retained. If $a=O$ the cap is oriented from its left lower leg to its right lower leg, and if $a=X$ the direction reverses. If $b=O$ the other strand enters from row $T$ and exits down column $Q$, and if $b=X$ this direction reverses. Every new corner's type is already prescribed in steps 2.1 and 7.1, so these four orientation cases require no unmarked or unoriented identification. Reflecting the entire labeled certificate horizontally or vertically preserves adjacency, disjointness, and strict interval containment and takes a three-mark stabilization block to another allowed such block. It also preserves which segments are vertical and hence which are over. It therefore supplies the stated opposite-side and minimum certificates; this does not assert a grid-move equivalence from a grid to its own reflection. Axis exchange is not used. The result is precisely the conditional finite certificate stated, with no claim about underpassing critical branches or general bridge rectification. Every operation is finite and needs no choice axiom.
